label: sec:double-slit-intro
html:
The double-slit experiment tests any quantum framework. It requires a single formalism that reproduces interference fringes, predicts their envelope, and explains coherence loss upon observation. In the QOU setting, the experiment splits into two scattering modes: photons and massive particles.

A massive particle propagates via the full q-Laplacian (particle). Its cross-coupling terms mix spatial and Reeb degrees of freedom to produce interference. A photon is background flux on the exceptional divisor (exceptional divisor). It carries color content \gamma = \mathbf{1} + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\sigma_0\sigma_1 (color content). The Hecke generators \sigma_0, \sigma_1 encode polarization. The color twist q\phi governs its phase. The color weights (\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_{01}) correct the interference envelope.

The two modes predict different envelope shapes: a q-corrected sinc{}^2 for massive particles, and a fractal Julia-set envelope for photons. Both recover classical Fraunhofer and Airy patterns at q = 1. At q \neq 1, band widths deviate. These anomalies match the Bach et al. [bach2013] 600 eV electron diffraction dataset.
